definition.text: The largest total amount of carbon dioxide humanity can still emit, added up over time, while keeping global warming below a chosen limit.

facts.text: Counted from the pre-industrial year 1750 it is the total carbon budget; counted from a recent date it is the remaining carbon budget.
It is also called an emissions budget, quota or allowable emissions.
Global warming rises almost in a straight line with cumulative carbon dioxide emissions, which is what makes a budget meaningful.
The warming that results does not depend on where the emissions come from and depends little on when they happen.
From 1750 to 2019 about 2390 gigatonnes of CO2 had already been emitted worldwide.
Estimates depend on the temperature target, the chosen probability of staying below it, and how far other greenhouse gases are cut too.
A 2023 update found 250 GtCO2 left from January 2023 for a 50% chance of staying below 1.5 °C, about 6 years of current emissions.
For a 50% chance of staying below 2 degrees, the same update gave 1220 GtCO2, about 30 years of current emissions.

title: Allocating national carbon budgets

definition.text: The question of how to split the world's carbon budget among countries, which requires value judgments about fairness.

facts.text: Nations differ in population, industrialisation, past emissions and ability to cut emissions, so scientists use principles of equity to divide the budget.
Under 'common but differentiated responsibilities', countries that emitted more in the past or are richer get smaller budgets.
The egalitarian principle shares budgets by population, which raises the question whether individuals have a right to pollute.
Grandfathering shares budgets by each nation's emissions in a base year; it was used under the Kyoto Protocol and the early EU ETS and favours developed countries.
Recent work argues grandfathering is not a standard of equity because it builds biases against poorer states.

contested_note: Scholars disagree about which equity principle should divide the budget, and some reject grandfathering outright.

definition.text: Deliberate human activity that takes carbon dioxide out of the air and stores it durably on land, underground, in the ocean or in products.

facts.text: It is also called carbon removal, greenhouse gas removal or negative emissions.
Net zero needs deep emission cuts first and then removal as well; removal counterbalances emissions that are hard to eliminate, such as some from farming and aviation.
Methods include afforestation, reforestation, carbon farming, bioenergy with carbon capture and storage, and direct air capture with storage.
Methods can be grouped by their place in the carbon cycle or by how long they store carbon, from decades to thousands of years.
As of 2023 about 2 gigatons of CO2 per year were removed, almost all by planting forests, equal to 4% of yearly human greenhouse gas emissions.
A 2019 NASEM report estimated that current safe and economic methods could remove up to 10 gigatons of CO2 per year if fully deployed.
Unlike removal, carbon capture and storage at a power plant cuts new emissions but does not lower the CO2 already in the air.

definition.text: How long carbon taken from the air stays stored before it might return to the atmosphere.

facts.text: Forests, kelp beds and other plants store carbon as they grow, but these stores are volatile because long-term storage cannot be guaranteed.
Wildfires, disease, economic pressure and changing politics can release stored carbon again.
Carbon can be stored more securely by injecting CO2 underground or locking it into insoluble carbonate salts.

definition.text: What it costs per tonne to remove carbon dioxide, which varies with how mature each method is and with the markets for removals and by-products.

facts.text: Direct air capture costs from $94 to $600 per tonne, biochar from $200 to $584, and nature-based solutions such as reforestation less than $50.
Biochar sells for more than nature-based removals because it stores carbon for hundreds or thousands of years, while forests are a more volatile store.
A direct air capture plant taking 1 MtCO2 a year uses 0.4–1.5 km2 of land, while roughly 46 million trees doing the same would need about 3,098–4,647 km2.
As of early 2023 financing fell short of what high-tech removal would need, and most new money came from voluntary private initiatives.
Concern exists because voluntary markets have historically been far smaller than markets created by government policy.

title: Carbon removal as moral hazard

definition.text: The worry that promises of future carbon removal could weaken efforts to cut emissions now.

facts.text: Critics stress that removal must not be treated as a substitute for cutting greenhouse gas emissions.
In 2018 relying on large-scale removal was seen as a major risk to the 1.5 °C goal, given uncertainty about how fast it can grow.
Removal plans in countries' 2023 climate pledges would need 1.2 billion hectares, as much land as all the world's cropland.
A 2019 NASEM report said that delaying mitigation because removal will provide a backstop misrepresents its real capacity.

contested_note: Critics see reliance on future removal as a risk that delays emission cuts, while it is also described as a needed complement for hard-to-abate sectors.

title: Marine carbon dioxide removal
article: Carbon dioxide removal#Marine carbon dioxide removal (mCDR)

definition.text: Methods that remove carbon dioxide through the ocean, whose dissolved carbon stays in balance with CO2 in the air.

facts.text: Ocean alkalinity enhancement dissolves minerals such as olivine or limestone so that carbonate settles on the sea floor, at an estimated US$100 to $150 per tonne.
Electrochemical methods can strip carbonate from seawater and are much cheaper when combined with desalination.
Ocean fertilization would store carbon for only 10–100 years.

definition.text: The storing of carbon in a carbon pool, a place in the Earth system where carbon stays for a period of time.

facts.text: By lowering the carbon dioxide in the air it helps manage the carbon cycle and limit climate change.
The two main types are biologic sequestration, also called biosequestration, and geologic sequestration.
Plants take carbon dioxide from the air as they grow and bind it into biomass; people can speed this up through land use and farming.
Biological stores such as forests may be temporary, since fires, disease, economic pressure and politics can release the carbon.
Injecting CO2 underground or turning it into carbonate salts locks carbon away for thousands to millions of years.
Within carbon capture and storage, sequestration is the storage step.
A 2025 study found that using all of Earth's geologic storage would limit warming by only 0.7 °C.

title: Biological carbon sequestration
article: Carbon sequestration#Biological carbon sequestration on land

definition.text: Capturing and storing atmospheric carbon dioxide through living processes, mainly plant growth, that people keep up and enhance.

facts.text: It works by raising photosynthesis through land uses such as reforestation and sustainable forest management.
Forests act as land carbon sinks, storing carbon in roots, stems, branches and leaves.
Converting natural land to cropland cuts soil organic carbon by about 30–40%.
Wetlands hold 20–30% of the world's soil carbon on only 5–8% of its land.

title: Geological carbon sequestration
article: Carbon sequestration#Underground storage in suitable geologic formations

definition.text: Storing carbon dioxide deep underground in depleted oil and gas fields, saline formations or coal beds that cannot be mined.

facts.text: Captured CO2 is compressed to about 100 bar, piped to the site and injected around 1 km deep, where it can stay for hundreds to millions of years.
A good site has porous, permeable rock such as sandstone under a tight cap rock such as shale.
Risks include CO2 leaking up along faults and earthquakes caused by too much pressure.
2025 research found that of nearly 12,000 GtCO2 of theoretical storage capacity, only 1,460 GtCO2 is risk-free.
Storage alone, without capture and transport, can cost below US$10 per tonne where onshore storage is available.

definition.text: Locking carbon dioxide into solid carbonate minerals by reacting it with metal oxides such as magnesium or calcium oxide.

facts.text: The same reaction happens slowly in nature and built up much of Earth's limestone over geologic time.
It can be sped up with heat, pressure, catalysts or by grinding minerals, but this needs extra energy.
CO2 dissolved in water and injected into hot basalt underground turns into solid carbonate minerals.

definition.text: Storing carbon by burying wood or other plant matter where it cannot rot, mimicking how fossil fuels formed.

facts.text: Its global potential is estimated at 10 ± 5 GtC per year, highest in tropical forests.
A 2008 estimate put wood burial costs at US$50 per tonne of carbon, much cheaper than capturing power-plant emissions.

title: Direct deep-sea CO2 injection
article: Carbon sequestration#Direct deep-sea carbon dioxide injection

definition.text: An abandoned idea of storing carbon dioxide by injecting it directly into the deep ocean for some centuries.

facts.text: Interest fell after about 2001 because of unknown effects on marine life, high costs and doubts about how long the carbon would stay.
The IPCC listed it in 2005 but no longer mentioned ocean storage in 2014.

definition.text: Action to limit the greenhouse gases in the atmosphere that cause climate change; also called decarbonisation.

facts.text: The IPCC defines it as a human intervention to reduce emissions or enhance the sinks of greenhouse gases.
Main actions are saving energy and replacing fossil fuels with clean energy; changing land use and removing CO2 are secondary strategies.
There are four types of measures: sustainable energy and transport, energy conservation, sustainable agriculture and green industry, and enhancing sinks and carbon removal.
2022 assessments said emissions must peak before 2025 and fall about 43% by 2030 to limit warming to 1.5 °C.
Adopted policies would still lead to about 2.7 °C of warming by 2100, well above the Paris Agreement goal.
Solar and wind can replace fossil fuels at the lowest cost of the renewable options.
Air travel and cement production are among the processes hardest to decarbonise.
Mitigation is often seen as a burden to share, but it can also be an opportunity for industrial development and exports.

definition.text: Cutting emissions by reducing demand for the goods and services that cause them, through behaviour, infrastructure and end-use technology.

facts.text: Examples include eating less meat, building good public transport and insulating houses.
Demand-side solutions could cut global greenhouse gas emissions by 40% to 70% by 2050 while improving well-being.
The richest 10% of people cause about half of all lifestyle emissions.
High-impact personal actions include flying less, avoiding petrol cars, eating mainly plants and electrifying homes.

definition.text: Eating fewer animal products and more plant-based food to cut the greenhouse gas emissions caused by food.

facts.text: Food is the largest share of consumption-based emissions, nearly 20% of the global carbon footprint.
Widespread vegetarian diets could cut food-related emissions by 63% by 2050.
Returning land used for animal farming to nature could sequester 100 billion tonnes of CO2 by 2100.

definition.text: Side benefits of cutting emissions beyond slowing climate change, such as cleaner air, better health, jobs and energy security; also called ancillary benefits.

facts.text: Fossil-fuel air pollution is estimated to kill over 5 million people a year as of 2019.
Replacing coal plants with renewables can more than double the jobs per megawatt of capacity in some cases.
Countries that import energy can gain independence and supply security by building renewables.
The IPCC noted in 2007 that co-benefits are often neglected and not quantified or monetised by decision-makers.
Counting co-benefits properly can change decisions about when and how much to mitigate.

definition.text: Harms and risks that some mitigation measures can cause, such as damage to biodiversity or mining pressure on conservation areas.

facts.text: Mining metals and minerals for renewable energy can threaten conservation areas.
Focusing on risks can produce deadlock, because people weigh possible losses more than benefits.

title: Sharing the costs of emissions cuts
article: Climate change mitigation#Distributing emissions abatement costs

definition.text: The question of how responsibility for cutting emissions, and its costs, should be divided among regions, income groups and sectors.

facts.text: Proposed principles include egalitarianism, basic needs, proportionality and the polluter-pays principle.
'Equal per capita entitlements' allocate emissions either by population or by also counting historical emissions.

definition.text: Countries' announced emission targets and how much warming they would lead to if carried out.

facts.text: In November 2021 Climate Action Tracker projected 2.7 °C of warming by 2100 under current policies.
Meeting all announced targets would make warming peak at 1.9 °C and fall to 1.8 °C by 2100.
Only the EU, UK, Chile and Costa Rica had detailed official plans for their 2030 targets.

title: Coal-to-gas switching
article: Climate change mitigation#Replacing coal with natural gas

definition.text: Replacing coal with natural gas to cut emissions in the short term.

facts.text: Burning gas gives about half the emissions of coal for electricity and about two-thirds for heat.
Methane leaks during extraction and transport can cancel out the gain.
It is no path to net zero, and new gas infrastructure risks carbon lock-in and stranded assets.

title: Preserving and enhancing carbon sinks
article: Climate change mitigation#Preserving and enhancing carbon sinks

definition.text: Managing Earth's natural carbon sinks so they keep or increase their ability to take CO2 from the air and store it durably.

facts.text: Globally the two most important carbon sinks are vegetation and the ocean.
Examples are preventing deforestation and restoring ecosystems by reforestation.
Ecosystem restoration and less land conversion are among the tools that can cut the most emissions before 2030.
The economic potential of forest and ecosystem measures is 4.2 to 7.4 GtCO2-eq per year.
The Stern Review said in 2007 that curbing deforestation was a highly cost-effective way to cut emissions.

definition.text: The grouping of emission cuts by the part of the economy where they happen: buildings, transport, industry, and agriculture, forestry and land use.

facts.text: Buildings account for 23% of global energy-related CO2 emissions; about half their energy goes to heating space and water.
Transport causes 15% of emissions; public transport, cycling, electric vehicles and rail help cut them.
Counting direct and indirect emissions, industry is the largest emitter; electrification, green hydrogen and circular economy measures can cut them.
Agriculture and forestry cause almost 20% of emissions, and cattle produce 21% of global methane.
A modern heat pump moves about three to five times more heat energy than the electricity it uses.

definition.text: The individual, institutional and market obstacles that hold back cutting emissions.

facts.text: Finance is a major barrier for land-based options, and accounting for carbon removal is an economic barrier.
Developing countries face a shortage of capital, which rose in cost in the early 2020s.
Only 0.12% of climate research funding goes to the social science of mitigation.

definition.text: The state in which greenhouse gas emissions from human activity are balanced by human removals; often shortened to net zero.

facts.text: Reaching net zero is needed to slow global warming, though gases already in the air keep causing some warming.
It needs deep emission cuts first; a small remaining share can then be balanced by carbon dioxide removal.
Net zero standards require cutting emissions by more than 90% and offsetting only the remaining 10% or less.
The idea grew from late-2000s research showing warming slows only when CO2 emissions reach net zero, and it underlies the Paris Agreement.
As of November 2023 about 145 countries had announced or were considering net zero targets, covering close to 90% of global emissions.
The IMF estimates that net zero by 2050 would leave global GDP 7 percent higher than current policies.
Net zero, carbon neutrality and climate neutrality are often used as synonyms, but some standards give them different meanings.

definition.text: Residual emissions are those not practical to cut for technical reasons; robust net zero rules say they must be balanced by removals that store carbon as long as the gas would last.

facts.text: Methane lasts around 12 years in the air, carbon dioxide between 300 and 1,000 years, so removals balancing CO2 must last much longer.
Avoided-emissions offsets cut emissions against a baseline but remove nothing from the air; weaker carbon neutrality standards allow them.
Critics worry offsets delay real emission cuts and aid greenwashing.

definition.text: The point that short-lived gases such as methane need not reach zero to halt warming, because cutting them lowers their warming effect at once.

facts.text: Net zero for CO2 alone can be reached sooner than for all greenhouse gases, partly because farm methane is harder to phase out.
Short-lived gases still push temperatures up in the short term and could breach 1.5 °C earlier.
Robust net zero standards cover all greenhouse gases, not only CO2.

title: Credibility of net-zero pledges

definition.text: The debate over whether net-zero targets are trustworthy, given that most are voluntary and lack enforcement.

facts.text: As of 2023 only 5% of companies with a net zero commitment had a credible plan, and credible targets covered only 7% of emissions.
Heavy reliance on carbon credits is a main reason many claims lack credibility.
The UN has condemned fossil fuel companies' net zero pledges, made while expanding production, as greenwashing.
Some climate scientists argue net zero lets actors put off cuts today by relying on unproven future technologies.

contested_note: Scientists and the UN question many net zero pledges, while standards bodies try to make them robust.

definition.text: A major structural change in how energy is supplied and used; today, the shift from fossil fuels to renewable and low-carbon energy.

facts.text: The current transition aims to cut energy emissions mainly by phasing down fossil fuels and running as much as possible on low-carbon electricity.
Energy production and use cause most human greenhouse gas emissions, and fossil fuels meet over three-quarters of energy needs.
An earlier transition took place in the Industrial Revolution, from wood and biomass to coal, then oil and gas.
The term arose after the 1973 oil crisis and was popularised by Jimmy Carter in 1977.
Falling solar and wind costs have driven the transition since the late 2010s.
Despite decades of climate policy, transitions have not sped up beyond historical trends and remain off track for climate targets.

title: Energy additions
article: Energy transition#Examples of past energy transitions

definition.text: The view that humanity has never truly switched energy sources but has kept adding new ones on top of old ones.

facts.text: One school, described by Vaclav Smil, sees successive transitions in the shares of the energy mix: biomass, coal, oil, then a mix.
Jean-Baptiste Fressoz's school notes that 19th-century coal did not replace wood; more wood was burned too.
As of 2024, use of all forms of primary energy had increased, leading some to call 'transition' a slogan.

contested_note: Historians disagree whether past energy changes were transitions or additions.

title: Falling cost of renewables
article: Energy transition#Cost competitiveness of renewable energies

definition.text: The steep drop in the cost of wind, solar and batteries that has made them the cheapest new power in many regions.

facts.text: From 2010 to 2019 unit costs fell 85% for solar, 55% for wind and 85% for lithium-ion batteries.
Onshore wind or solar with a few hours of storage already has lower levelized cost than gas peaking plants.
In 2021 renewables made up more than 80% of new electricity generating capacity.

title: Critical minerals for the energy transition

definition.text: Minerals needed for clean energy technologies, whose demand is set to rise steeply with the transition.

facts.text: The IEA lists 37 critical minerals and expects demand for them to rise 235 per cent by 2050.
For mineral-rich countries of Sub-Saharan Africa the transition may drive sustainable development.
Mining for these minerals can threaten conservation areas and contributed strongly to deforestation in 2023.

definition.text: How shifting energy sources changes the relations, dependencies and fortunes of countries and companies.

facts.text: Owners of fossil or renewable resources face big losses or gains depending on how the transition unfolds.
The transition is expected to reduce reliance on long-distance fossil fuel trade and raise the role of regional markets.
Energy security became a stronger driver in Europe after the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine.

definition.text: The aim that communities gain affordable, safe and sustainable energy and take part in decisions about it.

facts.text: It has procedural, distributive and recognition dimensions.
Distributive justice concerns how energy revenues, infrastructure sites and costs are shared; cities often gain while rural areas bear burdens.
Procedural justice requires transparent decisions and meaningful consultation.
Transitions may worsen energy insecurity for low-income households.
It aims to share the benefits and burdens of energy systems fairly across social groups, regions and generations.
Its three main tenets are distributive justice (where injustices arise), recognition justice (who is ignored) and procedural justice (how fair the process is).
Some scholars add restorative and cosmopolitan justice to capture international inequalities and harms from fossil fuels.
The energy justice cycle follows the energy system from extraction through production, supply and consumption to decommissioning and waste.

definition.text: The goal of meeting all energy use from renewable resources.

facts.text: It is motivated by emissions, pollution, and economic and energy security concerns.
Research on it is fairly new, with few studies before 2009.

definition.text: The principle that the shift to a low-carbon economy should treat people fairly and leave no workers, places or countries behind.

facts.text: It emerged in the 1980s from US trade unions protecting workers hit by environmental rules.
Tony Mazzocchi of the Oil, Chemical and Atomic Workers Union proposed a 'Superfund for Workers' to compensate and retrain them, and is believed to have coined the term.
Unions won just transition and decent work language in the Paris Agreement's preamble in 2015.
The IPCC stresses investing in low-emission industries, fair jobs, equitable energy access and economic diversification.
As of 2022, 38% of 170 countries referred to just transition in their short-term climate plans.
The EU's Just Transition mechanism helps fossil fuel-dependent regions move to a greener economy.

definition.text: An asset that has suffered an unexpected or early write-down, loss of value, or conversion into a liability.

facts.text: Stranding is part of the 'creative destruction' of growth and innovation and can carry risks for the whole financial system.
Climate change is expected to sharply increase stranded assets in carbon-intensive industries, with ripple effects through the world economy.
The IEA defines them as investments that stop earning a return before the end of their expected economic life because markets or rules change.
The term matters in financial risk management, to avoid losses once an asset has turned into a liability.

definition.text: The loss of value of assets such as fossil fuel reserves and carbon-intensive plants as climate policy, technology and markets shift.

facts.text: It affects oil, gas and coal companies and industries such as steel, aluminium and cement, and also fossil-exporting countries and workers.
Risk factors include environmental change, new regulations such as carbon pricing, falling clean-tech costs, changing social norms and litigation.
A 2021 study found nearly 60 percent of oil and gas reserves and 90 percent of coal reserves must stay unused for a 50 percent chance of 1.5°C.
A 2026 estimate found early closure of coal plants for a 1.5°C pathway would strand around $842 billion.
Net fossil fuel importers gain economically from switching to clean energy, while exporters face stranded assets.

definition.text: Rules that limit or discourage the extraction of natural resources such as fossil fuels, rather than only their use.

facts.text: It can replace or complement demand-side policy, which alone typically causes carbon leakage.
Bohm (1993) first showed that taking fossil fuel reserves off the market can be a beneficial climate policy.
Hoel (1994) showed the best policy combines demand- and supply-side tools, weighted by where leakage is larger, which depends on price elasticities.
Harstad (2012) showed a coalition can gain by buying and retiring fossil fuel reserves in other countries.
Supply-side treaties may be cheaper and easier to monitor, but major emitters are also major producers, so participation is still hard.
The Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative builds on this idea.

definition.text: A charcoal made by heating biomass with little oxygen, intended for use in soil and other organic uses.

facts.text: It is made by pyrolysis, heating biomass without oxygen, which yields solid biochar, liquid bio-oil and syngas.
In soil it can improve aeration and fertility, reduce nutrient leaching and acidity, and cut greenhouse gas emissions from the soil.
Too much, or the wrong feedstock, can harm soil life, change pH and raise salinity.
Because it is so stable, it can stay in soils for thousands of years, which underlies biochar carbon removal.
Pre-Columbian Amazonians made it by smouldering farm waste, creating soils settlers called terra preta.
It benefits degraded tropical soils more than temperate ones.
A 1–2% share of biochar works best in concrete, cutting emissions from cement.

verification.title: The use of Biochar to reduce the carbon footprint of cement-based materials
verification.evidence: Based on previous work, this investigation has a twofold objective: to understand the full influence of the use of an optimized percentage of Biochar (2% with respect to the weight of the cement) either as a filler in the mixture or as a substitute for cement, while guaranteeing an improvement in th

definition.text: A tropical farming method that chars cleared vegetation into biochar instead of burning it, as an alternative to slash-and-burn.

facts.text: Slash-and-burn leaves only 3% of the plant carbon in the soil, while slash-and-char can keep up to 50%.
Switching worldwide could sequester 0.22 to 0.42 Gt C per year.
Biochar soils stay productive, unlike depleted slash-and-burn fields that push farmers to clear more land.

title: Biochar carbon removal

definition.text: A negative emissions method that turns leftover biomass into biochar by pyrolysis and stores it in soil or durable materials; also called pyrogenic carbon capture and storage.

facts.text: Plants take CO2 from the air as they grow; pyrolysis locks that carbon into a stable form that can last centuries to millennia.
Biomass is heated to 350–900 °C with little oxygen, giving biochar plus bio-oil and pyrogas.
In 2022/2023 it accounted for 87–92% of all delivered carbon removals.
Its potential is put at 0.3 to 4.9 billion tonnes of CO2 per year.
It is seen as quick to deploy and capital-efficient, suited to farmers and rural diversification in developing countries.
Some studies report fast decay or more soil emissions, though a 2025 re-analysis says common decay models overestimate decay.

contested_note: Studies disagree on how fast biochar carbon decays in soil, partly because of disputed decay models.

definition.text: Carbon credits earned by certified biochar carbon removal and sold in carbon markets.

facts.text: Because abatement costs are high, biochar credits trade about an order of magnitude above credits from emission cuts or nature-based solutions.
In 2024 biochar projects made up 86% of the volume of carbon dioxide removal purchases.
To be certified, suppliers must be carbon net-negative, storing more carbon than they use making and distributing biochar.

title: Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage
article: Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage

definition.text: Getting energy from biomass and capturing and storing the carbon dioxide this produces; known as BECCS.

facts.text: Growing plants absorb CO2; when their energy is used, some CO2 is captured and stored underground, so BECCS can remove CO2 from the air under some conditions.
Its negative emissions potential has been estimated at zero to 22 gigatonnes a year.
Cost estimates range from $60 to $250 per ton of CO2.
As of 2024 only 3 large-scale BECCS projects operated worldwide.
Large-scale biomass growing risks breaching planetary boundaries through land and water scarcity, biodiversity loss, competition with food and deforestation.
Using farm and forestry residues instead of energy crops avoids many of these problems.

sources.title: Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage

title: Carbon capture technologies
article: Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage#Technology

definition.text: The three main ways to capture CO2 from burning fuel: post-combustion, pre-combustion and oxy-fuel combustion.

facts.text: Post-combustion separates CO2 from flue gas after burning and can be retrofitted to existing plants.
Pre-combustion gasifies fuel into syngas and captures CO2 before power is made.
Oxy-fuel combustion burns fuel in oxygen and recycled flue gas, giving a CO2-rich exhaust.
Expected efficiencies are 95% for post-combustion, 85% for pre-combustion and 87.5% for oxy-combustion.

sources.title: Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage

definition.text: A family of carbon removal methods that collect biomass, such as farm waste, and store its carbon permanently or semi-permanently; known as BiCRS.

facts.text: Unlike direct air capture, which is costly and energy-hungry, it relies on photosynthesis and then engineering to store the carbon-rich residue.
It includes BECCS and biochar carbon removal.
Challenges include measuring the carbon stored in buried biomass and extra demand for farmland, so think tanks urge limits on which biomass may be used.

title: Carbon capture and storage

definition.text: Separating carbon dioxide from industrial sources before it reaches the air and moving it to long-term storage, usually deep underground; known as CCS.

facts.text: Around 80% of captured CO2 is used for enhanced oil recovery, so CCS is also called carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS).
Capture usually passes exhaust through an amine solvent that binds CO2.
As of 2023 CCS captured around 0.1% of global emissions, about 45 million tonnes of CO2.
Capture costs US$15–25 per tonne for concentrated streams such as gas processing but US$40–120 for dilute streams from power, cement and steel plants.
Compared with other ways to cut emissions it is very expensive; many options cost under US$20 per tonne.
Site-specific designs limit cost cuts through learning-by-doing.
The literature gives CCS a small but critical role, while fossil fuel companies promote it to extend the fossil era, making it politically divisive.

contested_note: CCS remains politically divisive, with disagreement over its cost-effectiveness and whether it prolongs fossil fuel use.

title: Enhanced oil recovery with captured CO2
article: Carbon capture and storage#Emissions with enhanced oil recovery

definition.text: Injecting captured CO2 into old oil fields to push out more oil, and the dispute over whether this helps or harms the climate.

facts.text: Counting the emissions from burning the extra oil, capture with EOR usually increases total emissions; leaving them out, it reduces them.
A 2020 review found scientific papers roughly evenly split on the question.
The IEA estimates 80% of EOR oil displaces other oil, giving 0.13 tonnes of CO2 from burning per tonne stored.

contested_note: Studies are split on whether CO2-based enhanced oil recovery raises or lowers net emissions.

title: Energy penalty of CCS
article: Carbon capture and storage#Energy and water requirements

definition.text: The extra energy a facility uses to capture, compress and store its CO2.

facts.text: Early studies found a coal plant needs 14–40% more coal and a gas plant 11–22% more gas for the same electricity.
Burning more fuel raises upstream harms such as mining and methane leaks, and can increase local air pollution.
Coal plants with CCS may need 50% more water.

title: Unabated fossil fuels
article: Carbon capture and storage#Fossil fuel abatement

definition.text: Fossil fuels burned without measures, such as carbon capture, that substantially cut their emissions.

facts.text: Negotiators have argued over phasing out all fossil fuels or only 'unabated' ones.
The 2023 UN climate conference agreed to phase down unabated coal but left 'abated' undefined, which critics say invites abuse.
The IPCC counts power plants as abated only if they capture 90% or more of emissions.

contested_note: Countries disagree whether phase-out targets should cover all fossil fuels or only unabated ones.

title: Carbon capture and utilization
article: Carbon capture and storage#CO2 use in products

definition.text: Using captured CO2 as a raw material for products instead of storing it.

facts.text: As of 2022 products used only around 1% of the CO2 captured each year.
In urea fertilizer production, CO2 from the process is often recycled.

definition.text: Stopping the burning of coal in power plants and elsewhere, as part of the fossil fuel phase-out.

facts.text: Coal is the most carbon-intensive fossil fuel; the IEA estimates it caused over 30% of warming above pre-industrial levels.
Coal power emits about a tonne of CO2 per megawatt hour, twice as much as gas.
Its health and environmental benefits exceed its costs, by over 1% of GDP a year according to one estimate.
Economists have suggested a Coasean bargain in which developed countries help pay for developing countries' coal phase-out.
The IEA 1.5°C pathway would require closing around 70% of existing coal capacity early.
Germany uses reverse auctions to pay coal plants to close early, and some countries retire coal miners early as part of a just transition.
Coal phase-down was agreed in the 2021 Glasgow Climate Pact.

definition.text: The point of highest coal consumption, after which use is expected to decline.

facts.text: Once expected to come from running out of reserves, peak coal is now driven by falling demand as climate policy and cheaper gas and renewables spread.
Coal's share of global energy peaked in 2008 at 30%.
Use is falling in the US and Europe but rising in India, Indonesia and China.

title: Direct air capture

definition.text: Using chemical or physical processes to pull carbon dioxide straight out of the surrounding air; with long-term storage it is called DACCS.

facts.text: Unlike CCS, which captures CO2 at a source such as a factory, it lowers the CO2 concentration of the atmosphere as a whole.
Fans push air past liquid solvents or solid sorbents that bind CO2; heat then releases a concentrated CO2 stream and regenerates the material.
In 2025 costs exceeded $1000 per tonne, many times the carbon price, so it is not yet part of emissions trading.
Economies of scale could bring costs to $94–232 per tonne for a 1 Mtpa plant, though some dispute that costs can fall below $200.
It uses about 1 to 2.5 MWh of electricity per tonne of CO2.
Its own emissions range from 0.01 tCO2 per tCO2 captured with renewable power to 0.65 with grid power and gas heat.
Climate campaigners criticise it as a costly distraction from cutting emissions that helps keep the fossil fuel industry going.

contested_note: Experts dispute how far its costs can fall, and campaigners question whether it serves climate goals or prolongs fossil fuel use.
notes: Cost figures differ by plant scale and date (over $1000 today, $94–232 projected at 1 Mtpa; CDR page gives $94–600): these are different quantities, not conflicts.

definition.text: Switching to electricity as the power source; in sustainable energy, moving end uses like transport and heating onto clean electricity.

facts.text: Clean energy such as renewables and nuclear is mostly produced as electricity, so end uses must be electrified for a sustainable energy system.
Electric vehicles and heat pumps are two key areas.
The National Academy of Engineering called it the greatest engineering achievement of the 20th Century.
Electrification and economic growth are highly correlated; 1900 to 1940 was a period of high productivity growth.
About 840 million people, mostly in Africa, had no grid electricity in 2017, down from 1.2 billion in 2010.
Electricity is a 'sticky', multi-source form of energy, resilient in the long term but unstable in the short term because supply must match use instantly.

definition.text: Replacing fuel-burning vehicles with electric ones to make transport more sustainable.

facts.text: Producing electricity sustainably is easier than producing liquid fuels sustainably.
Hydrogen may suit long-distance lorries, while shipping and aviation may rely more on sustainable liquid fuels.

definition.text: Switching space, water and industrial heating from burning fuels to electricity, mainly heat pumps.

facts.text: The IEA estimates heat pumps provide only 5% of global space and water heating but could provide over 90%.
Industrial processes needing very high temperatures, such as 900 °C for ethylene, need new electric processes.
Many households cannot afford enough heating or cooling, and existing heating is often polluting.

definition.text: Speeding up natural rock weathering by spreading finely ground silicate rock, such as basalt, so it reacts with water and air and removes carbon dioxide.

facts.text: The CO2 ends up stored in solid carbonate minerals or as ocean alkalinity, which also slows ocean acidification.
In nature, rainwater and CO2 form carbonic acid that slowly dissolves minerals; over geological time this helps stabilise Earth's climate.
It could remove 2–4 Gt of CO2 per year.
A 2020 analysis put the cost on cropland at US$80–180 per tonne of CO2, comparable to BECCS and large-scale direct air capture.
Uncertain mineral dissolution rates make its cost and speed uncertain.
Mine tailings and industrial wastes like steel slag can be used first, but more basalt mining might eventually be needed.

definition.text: The proposed gradual reduction of fossil fuel use and production to zero, to cut air pollution, limit climate change and gain energy independence.

facts.text: Fossil fuels cause over 70% of greenhouse gas emissions, so phasing them out is the largest part of limiting warming.
Policies include demand-side measures that cut consumption and supply-side measures that limit production.
Alternatives include electrification, green hydrogen and biofuel.
Most premature deaths from air pollution are due to fossil fuels, and the monetised health benefits of phase-out exceed the cost of the 2 °C goal.
Governments subsidised fossil fuels by about $500 billion a year as of 2019; the IMF's wider definition gave $5.2 trillion in 2017.
As of 2024 global fossil fuel use was still increasing, continuing the trend since 1965.
Workers and politicians tied to fossil fuel industries tend to oppose phase-out unless they have strong alternatives.

title: Phase-out of fossil fuel vehicles
article: Fossil fuel phase-out#Phase-out of fossil fuel vehicles

definition.text: Bans on selling new petrol and diesel vehicles, requiring new cars to be electric or otherwise zero-emission.

facts.text: Many countries have set dates to stop selling petrol and diesel cars, but no timetable exists for ending fossil gas burning.
Many US states have zero-emission vehicle mandates requiring a rising share of electric car sales.

definition.text: Deliberate large-scale intervention in Earth's climate system to counteract human-caused climate change; also called climate engineering.

facts.text: It usually covers two categories: large-scale carbon dioxide removal and solar radiation modification.
Carbon removal is generally counted as mitigation, while SRM reflects some sunlight back to space.
The two differ greatly in mechanisms, timelines and risks and are now usually discussed separately.
A common objection is that focusing on these technologies could undermine efforts to cut emissions.
Effective governance and international oversight are widely seen as essential.

definition.text: Proposed interventions to slow the loss of glaciers, ice sheets and sea ice.

facts.text: They are motivated by fears that feedbacks such as ice-albedo loss could trigger climate tipping points.
Methods include regional sunlight reflection, reflective surfaces, draining water under glaciers and seabed curtains.
The research is early and effectiveness is highly uncertain.

definition.text: The international rules and agreements that address geoengineering, mostly specific to each method.

facts.text: In 2010 the Convention on Biological Diversity set a non-binding framework requiring scientific justification, environmental assessment and oversight.
A 2013 London Protocol amendment created a binding framework for marine geoengineering, starting with ocean fertilization, but it has not entered into force.

definition.text: A record of the greenhouse gases emitted, and removed by carbon sinks, in a country, region or organisation.

facts.text: Scientists use inventories in atmospheric models; policy makers use them to design and track emission cuts.
Unlike other air emission inventories, they also count removals by carbon sinks.
Parties to the UNFCCC and the Kyoto Protocol must submit annual inventories of human emissions and removals.
The simplest method multiplies an amount of activity, such as fuel burned, by an 'emission factor'.
Almost all countries are parties to the Paris Agreement, which requires regular production-based inventories.

title: Production- and consumption-based emissions accounting
article: Greenhouse gas inventory#Greenhouse gas emissions accounting

definition.text: The two main ways to count a country's emissions: production-based counts emissions made on its territory, consumption-based counts those caused by what it consumes, including imports.

facts.text: Production-based accounting includes exports but excludes imports; consumption-based does the reverse.
Production-based accounting is favoured in policy because it is easier to measure, but it misses emissions embodied in trade.
Consumption-based accounting uses multi-regional input-output models to trace products through global supply chains.
It is more uncertain and data-hungry and needs more international cooperation.
Under production accounting a country with polluting exports, like Norway where 69% of CO2 comes from export production, could meet targets just by exporting less.

contested_note: The literature disagrees which accounting method is fairer and better for policy, and some propose sharing responsibility.

title: Emissions embodied in trade
article: Greenhouse gas inventory#Emissions embodied in international trade

definition.text: Greenhouse gases released making goods in one country that are consumed in another.

facts.text: Traded emissions totalled 7.8 Gt in 2008, with a net 1.6 Gt CO2 flowing from developing to developed countries.
Developed countries seemed to stabilise their domestic emissions from 1990 to 2008, but this is misleading once rising imports from developing countries are counted.
Production-based accounting shows lower emissions for EU and OECD countries; consumption-based shows the reverse.

title: Shared emissions responsibility

definition.text: The proposal that emissions be split between importing and exporting countries at each stage of the supply chain.

facts.text: It argues the consumer starts production, but the producing country also gains GDP from it.
Disagreement remains over the criteria; Lenzen et al. propose shares proportional to value added.

contested_note: Researchers have not agreed on the criteria for splitting responsibility.

definition.text: The economic idea that productivity rises through practice, self-improvement and small innovations.

facts.text: An example is a factory that produces more by learning to use its equipment better, without more workers or capital.
It was first measured in World War II bomber production, where costs fell with cumulative output rather than current volume.
This explains the non-linear cost falls seen in semiconductors and solar PV.
Kenneth Arrow used it in endogenous growth theory; Robert Lucas used it to explain increasing returns to human capital.
Learning economies are proportional to cumulative production, the experience curve.

definition.text: An economy that absorbs as much greenhouse gas as it emits, or more broadly one whose activities produce far lower emissions.

facts.text: Similar terms include green economy, carbon-neutral economy and decarbonised economy; 'carbon' stands for all greenhouse gases.
Getting there means cutting emissions in every sector, through renewables, efficiency, electric vehicles, heat pumps and climate-smart agriculture.
It needs energy policies and financial incentives such as emissions trading and carbon taxes.
Besides mitigation it brings benefits for ecosystems, trade, jobs, health, energy security and competitiveness.
Workers in carbon-intensive industries are more likely to lose jobs, while new jobs come from renewables and building renovation.
Switching to lower-emission technologies often pays back within 0.5–5 years.
Climate change is often framed as a free-rider problem: each country gains from others' mitigation but loses by going low-carbon alone.

definition.text: Electricity produced with far lower lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions than fossil fuel power.

facts.text: Sources include wind, solar, nuclear and most hydropower; fossil plants count only when fitted with carbon capture.
Almost 40% of global electricity came from low-carbon sources in 2020: about 10% nuclear, almost 10% wind and solar, and around 20% hydro and other renewables.
Very little comes from fossil sources, mostly because carbon capture is costly.
Moving to low-carbon power is among the most important actions to limit climate change.

title: Nuclear power in decarbonisation

definition.text: The disagreement over whether expanding nuclear power is needed to reach a low-carbon economy.

facts.text: The IEA, the IAEA and the UN Economic Commission for Europe hold that decarbonisation is not possible without some nuclear expansion.
Nuclear is low-carbon but carries risks and rising costs.
Environmental and security risks could outweigh its benefits.

contested_note: Agencies see nuclear expansion as necessary, while others stress its risks and costs.

title: Solar radiation modification

definition.text: Large-scale methods to limit global warming by reflecting more sunlight away from Earth back to space; also called solar geoengineering.

facts.text: It is meant to complement, not replace, cuts in greenhouse gas emissions.
Models consistently show it could reduce warming and many climate effects, but effects would vary by region and season.
It is the only known way to lower global temperatures within months.
Direct costs could be billions to tens of billions of US dollars per degree Celsius of cooling, low compared with climate damages.
It does not lower CO2, so it does nothing about ocean acidification.
Some fear it would weaken the will to cut emissions, a 'moral hazard' whose size experts dispute.
Low cost and feasibility mean one country could deploy it alone, and no comprehensive global framework regulates it.

contested_note: Scientists, NGOs and governments disagree on whether SRM should be researched or deployed at all.

definition.text: Putting small reflective particles into the upper atmosphere to reflect sunlight and cool the planet.

facts.text: It is the most-researched SRM method; the IPCC found high agreement it could limit warming to below 1.5 °C.
Sulfates are the usual proposal because volcanic eruptions release them naturally.
A key risk is delaying the recovery of the ozone layer.

definition.text: Spraying tiny sea-water droplets into low ocean clouds to make them reflect more sunlight.

facts.text: Its cooling would be felt quickly and could be reversed on fairly short time scales.
Technical barriers remain, it could not offset all current warming, and its risks are unclear.

definition.text: The rapid warming that would follow if solar radiation modification masking much warming were stopped suddenly.

facts.text: Abrupt termination with high greenhouse gas levels would bring fast temperature rise, sea level rise and weaker carbon sinks.
Large-scale SRM would likely need a commitment of decades to a century.
The IPCC notes a gradual phase-out with mitigation would reduce the impact.

title: Sustainable energy

definition.text: Energy that meets present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs, judged by its effects on environment, economy and society.

facts.text: Its impacts range from greenhouse gas emissions and air pollution to energy poverty and toxic waste.
Fossil fuels provide 85% of world energy use, and the energy system causes 76% of greenhouse gas emissions.
Renewables like wind, hydro, solar and geothermal can harm the environment but are generally far more sustainable than fossil fuels.
The role of non-renewables is controversial: nuclear avoids carbon and air pollution but brings waste, proliferation and accident risks.
Around 790 million people lack electricity and 2.6 billion cook with polluting fuels such as wood or charcoal.
Energy efficiency could deliver 40% of the emission cuts needed for the Paris Agreement, according to the IEA.
The IPCC estimates US$2.4 trillion a year must be invested in the energy system from 2016 to 2035 to limit warming to 1.5 °C.

contested_note: Whether non-renewable sources such as nuclear and natural gas belong in sustainable energy is disputed.

definition.text: Energy sources that are naturally replenished, such as solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, bioenergy and marine energy.

facts.text: They generally strengthen energy security and emit far fewer greenhouse gases than fossil fuels.
Hydropower is the largest renewable electricity source; it supplied 17% of world electricity in 2020.
Wind provided well over 10% of global electricity in 2024, and onshore wind is often cheaper than existing coal plants.
Solar PV is expected to have the largest installed capacity of any electricity source by 2027.
Projects can threaten biodiversity when high-value areas become bioenergy, wind or solar farms.

title: Sustainability of bioenergy

definition.text: The question of whether energy from plant and animal material really cuts emissions, given how biomass is grown and sourced.

facts.text: Biomass can be burned for heat and power or made into biofuels such as biodiesel and ethanol.
Land-use change, cultivation and processing can make bioenergy emit more carbon overall than fossil fuels.
Energy crops can displace ecosystems, degrade soils, use water and compete with food production.
Algae, waste and crops on land unfit for food are relatively sustainable sources.

contested_note: Bioenergy's climate benefit depends heavily on feedstock and land use, and in some cases it emits more than fossil fuels.

definition.text: Using cleanly produced hydrogen gas as a fuel where cheaper low-carbon options are scarce, such as heavy industry and long-distance transport.

facts.text: Almost all hydrogen today comes from fossil fuels by steam methane reforming, emitting 6.6–9.3 tonnes of CO2 per tonne of hydrogen.
Splitting water with clean electricity gives sustainable hydrogen, but costs more and converts energy inefficiently.
It can supply the intense heat for steel, cement and glass, and replace coke in steelmaking.

definition.text: Replacing polluting cooking fuels such as wood and dung with clean facilities.

facts.text: Polluting cooking fuels release harmful smoke and can drive forest degradation.
Cooking with biomass plus fossil fuel pollution causes an estimated 7 million deaths a year.
Universal clean cooking would greatly improve health with minimal effect on climate.

definition.text: Raising the money for innovation and investment that the energy transition needs.

facts.text: Required investment, about 2.5% of world GDP, is small compared with the economic and health benefits, most studies find.
Underfunding is acute in least developed countries, which attract little private investment.
Developed countries' Paris pledge of an extra $100 billion a year for poor countries has not been met.
Ending fossil fuel subsidies could cut global carbon emissions by 28% and air pollution deaths by 46%.

title: Emissions gap

definition.text: The difference between the emission cuts countries have pledged and the cuts needed to meet a temperature goal, tracked in UNEP's annual Emissions Gap Report.

facts.text: UNEP first assessed in November 2010 a gap between Copenhagen Accord pledges and the cuts needed for a likely chance of meeting 2 °C.
The 2022 Emissions Gap Report said emissions needed to be almost halved.
The 2024 report found current policies would likely lead to 3.1 °C of warming, and full pledges to 1.9 °C.
The 2020 report said 1.5 °C needs a 57% global cut from 2019 levels by 2030.

notes: Phrase concept; mentioned on several in-scope pages (Climate change mitigation, Greenhouse gas, Greenhouse gas emissions, Copenhagen climate summit, Solar radiation modification).
